title: Reverse Words in a String
description: Brute force to optimized: split/reverse/join versus a manual backward scan versus the reverse-all-then-reverse-parts in place trick.

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement
Problem Summary: Given a string s containing words separated by spaces, return a string with the words in reverse order, joined by a single space, with no leading, trailing, or extra interior spaces.

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

blocks.text: 2. Pattern Detection

blocks.content: {"headers":["Field","Detail"],"rows":[["Pattern","Reverse the entire string, then reverse each word segment back individually, then compact extra spaces with a read and write pointer."],["Difficulty","Intermediate"],["Tags","Strings, Two Pointers"],["Interview Focus","Recognizing that reversing a whole sequence and then reversing its meaningful sub-pieces back reorders chunks without needing any extra storage."]]}

blocks.text: 3. Understand the Problem
Given a string s containing words separated by spaces, return a string with the words in reverse order, joined by a single space, with no leading, trailing, or extra interior spaces.

blocks.title: Analogy: Reading a Sentence Backward, Word by Word
blocks.text: Like reading a sentence backward one whole word at a time, rather than one letter at a time, and cleaning up any extra gaps left over from the original spacing along the way.

blocks.caption: The order of whole words reverses, and every gap becomes exactly one space

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples
Example: s = "the sky is blue"

blocks.text: Example: s = "  hello world  "

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["Leading and trailing spaces are ignored entirely","only the two words hello and world matter","surrounding whitespace carries no meaning and must be discarded"],["Answer","\"world hello\"","the two words reversed with no leftover leading or trailing spaces"]]}

blocks.text: Edge case: s = "a good   example"
Multiple spaces between words in the input collapse down to exactly one space in the output, giving "example good a".
5. How Should We Think?
It helps to ask whether reversing the words really requires building and reversing a separate list at all.

blocks.title: How Should We Think?
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Splitting on whitespace, reversing the resulting list, and rejoining works, since the library split call automatically collapses any amount of surrounding or interior spacing, but it hides the actual word boundary mechanics behind several intermediate structures.

Observation 2: Scanning manually from the very end of the string backward, skipping spaces and then walking backward through one whole word at a time, builds the reversed order directly in a single pass, with no separate list or reverse step needed.

Observation 3: Rotate Array already showed that reversing an entire sequence, then reversing each of its meaningful sub-pieces back, reorders chunks without any extra storage; the same trick applies here, reversing the whole string first (which correctly reorders the words but scrambles each word's own letters), then reversing each individual word segment back to fix its letters.

Observation 4: Move Zeroes already showed the "read pointer scans forward, write pointer only advances when something needs to be kept" compaction idea; that exact same read and write pointer technique compacts away every extra space in one more pass, confirmed by tracing s equal to "the sky is blue" through the full reverse-then-reverse-then-compact pipeline to the correct answer, "blue is sky the".

Recognizing that reversing everything and then reversing the meaningful pieces back reorders chunks without extra storage is what turns this from a split-and-rebuild problem into a fully in place one.
6. Brute Force Solution

Split the string on whitespace using a library function, which automatically discards empty pieces caused by multiple spaces, reverse the resulting list of words, and join them back together with a single space.
Step by step algorithm

items: Split the string on any run of whitespace, discarding empty results.
Reverse the resulting list of words.
Join the reversed list back into a single string with one space between each word.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: The library split call handles leading, trailing, and multiple interior spaces automatically, discarding every resulting empty piece.
Reversing the list of words directly reorders them without needing to touch any individual word's own characters.
Joining with a single space guarantees the required clean spacing in the final result.

blocks.text: 7. Analyze the Brute Force
The split call correctly collapses any amount of surrounding or interior whitespace, and reversing the resulting word list correctly reorders them.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), for the split, reverse, and join operations.
Space: O(n), for the intermediate list of words.

Limitation: relying entirely on library functions hides the actual mechanics of word boundary detection, and builds several intermediate structures (the split list, the reversed list) instead of producing the answer more directly in one coordinated pass.
8. Optimize the Solution

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why the brute force works but is opaque: it delegates word boundary detection entirely to a library call, then builds a full intermediate list just to reverse it and rejoin it.

What a manual backward scan fixes directly: walking from the end of the string, skipping spaces and capturing one whole word at a time, produces the words in the exact reversed order needed, with no separate reverse step.

What can be removed on top of that: in a language with mutable strings, even the manual word-by-word extraction can be replaced by reversing the whole string and then reversing each word segment back.

The core idea: scan manually to remove reliance on library magic first, then, where possible, apply the reverse-everything-then-reverse-the-pieces trick to avoid any extra storage at all.

Scan the string manually from the very end toward the beginning. At each step, skip over any spaces, then walk backward through one whole word, capture it, and append it directly onto the result along with a single separating space, moving on to look for the next word further back. This directly builds the reversed order in a single manual pass, without a separate split step followed by a separate reverse step.
9. Optimized Solution
Scan from the end of the string, manually extracting each word and appending it to the result in the order encountered.
Dry run for s = "the sky is blue"

blocks.content: {"headers":["Scan direction","Word extracted","Result so far"],"rows":[["from the end","blue","\"blue\""],["continuing backward","is","\"blue is\""],["continuing backward","sky","\"blue is sky\""],["continuing backward","the","\"blue is sky the\""]]}

blocks.caption: Optimized: scan backward from the end, extracting one whole word at a time

blocks.text: Why This Works

This works because scanning backward and extracting one complete word at a time naturally visits the words in the exact reversed order the answer needs, so appending each one directly to the result as it is found builds the final answer in a single pass with no separate reversal step required afterward.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","What Happens","Result"],"rows":[["A run of one or more spaces is encountered while scanning backward","The scan simply continues past them without recording anything","Any amount of surrounding or interior whitespace is correctly ignored"],["A complete word is found between two space runs (or a space and the string boundary)","It is captured and appended to the result immediately","Words appear in the result in exactly the reversed order they were encountered"]]}

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), a single backward pass with each character visited a constant number of times.
Space: O(n), for the result string being built.
10. Further Optimization: Reverse Whole, Then Reverse Each Word Back

In languages where the string is mutable in place (like a character array in C++), an elegant alternative avoids allocating any separate word list at all: first reverse the entire string. This puts every word in the correct final order but with each individual word's own letters backward. A second pass then reverses each individual word segment back to its correct letter order. Finally, a two pointer compaction pass, writing over the string in place, removes any extra spaces, using only the space the answer itself needs.
Dry run for s = "the sky is blue"

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Result"],"rows":[["Reverse the entire string","\"eulb si yks eht\""],["Reverse each individual word segment back","\"blue is sky the\""],["Compact any extra spaces (already clean in this example)","\"blue is sky the\""]]}

blocks.caption: Further optimization: reverse everything, then reverse each word back, all in place

blocks.text: Code walkthrough

items: Reversing the entire string first correctly moves every word into its final reversed order, as a side effect also reversing each word's own internal letter order.
Reversing each individual word segment, identified by scanning for space boundaries, back to its correct order undoes exactly that side effect, without disturbing the now-correct word order.

The final compaction pass uses a read pointer and a write pointer, exactly the Move Zeroes technique, to collapse any run of spaces down to a single separator, using only as much space as the final clean answer needs.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), three linear passes (reverse all, reverse each word, compact spaces).
Space: O(1) extra in a language with mutable strings, since everything is rearranged directly within the existing character buffer.
11. Complexity Comparison

blocks.content: {"headers":["Solution","Time","Space","Extra Storage","Interview Recommendation"],"rows":[["Brute force (split, reverse, join)","O(n)","O(n)","A full list of split words","Correct and simple, relies on library behavior."],["Optimized (manual backward scan)","O(n)","O(n)","The result string being built","Shows the underlying mechanics explicitly, still needs O(n) space."],["Further optimized (reverse all, reverse each word, compact)","O(n)","O(1) extra (mutable strings only)","None beyond the existing character buffer","The strongest answer where string mutation in place is possible."]]}

blocks.text: 12. Key Takeaways

The "reverse everything, then reverse the pieces back" trick is a general technique for reordering chunks of a sequence in place, and reappears in problems like rotating an array, where the same three reversal idea produces the rotation without any extra array.
Common Mistakes

items: Forgetting to trim leading and trailing spaces before processing, which can leave stray spaces in the final answer.
Not collapsing multiple interior spaces down to exactly one, producing an answer with extra gaps between words.

blocks.text: Edge Cases

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","Expected Behavior"],"rows":[["A string that is entirely spaces","Should produce an empty result."],["A single word with no spaces at all","Simply returned unchanged."]]}

blocks.text: Interview Tips

Clarify up front whether the language's strings are mutable, since that determines whether the true O(1) extra space in place trick is even applicable, or whether an O(n) space approach using a list of words is the practical choice.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text:
If the interviewer says "can you do this without extra space", think: reverse the whole string, then reverse each word back, then compact spaces, all in place (in a mutable string language).
If the interviewer says "what if the language's strings are immutable", think: a manual backward scan building the result directly is the practical O(n) space answer.
If the interviewer says "how do you remove the extra spaces cleanly", think: the same read pointer, write pointer compaction technique used in Move Zeroes.
Interview Follow-up Questions

items: Why does reversing the whole string first, then reversing each word segment back, correctly reorder the words while preserving each word's own letter order?
How does the space compaction pass relate to the technique used in Move Zeroes?
How would you reverse only the order of characters within each word, without changing the order of the words themselves?
How would this approach need to change if words could be separated by multiple different kinds of whitespace, such as tabs and newlines?
How would you reverse the words in a string that is presented as a stream of characters, where you cannot look ahead or go back?

blocks.text: Pattern Connections

items: Rotate Array, whose reverse-everything-then-reverse-the-pieces trick is applied here directly to whole words instead of array segments.
Move Zeroes, whose read and write pointer compaction technique is reused directly in the final space-collapsing pass here.
Reverse a String and Reverse Vowels of a String, whose in place two pointer swap is the building block behind reversing both the whole string and each individual word segment here.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: Brute force (split, reverse, join): O(n) time, O(n) space. Optimized (manual backward scan): O(n) time, O(n) space. Further optimized (reverse whole, then reverse each word, then compact): O(n) time, O(1) extra space in a mutable string language.
13. Final Summary

items: Pattern: reverse the entire string, then reverse each word segment back individually, then compact extra spaces with a read and write pointer.
Core Idea: reversing a whole sequence and then reversing its meaningful sub-pieces back reorders chunks in place, and a read/write pointer pass collapses any leftover extra spacing.
Time: O(n) for all three approaches.
Space: O(n) for the brute force and the manual scan, O(1) extra for the fully in place further optimization in a mutable string language.

Most Important Observation: reordering chunks of a sequence and fixing each chunk's own internal order are two separable steps, which is exactly what makes the reverse-all-then-reverse-pieces trick work.
Interview Difficulty: the split-reverse-join version is trivial; the fully in place version, and explaining why it is correct, is what shows deeper understanding.
One line memory trick: reverse it all, reverse each word back, then compact the gaps.
